items.title: Your cell membranes are 200,000 volts per centimetre
items.claim: The inner mitochondrial membrane has a voltage of about 150 mV across its 5-nanometre thickness. Scaled up, that's an electric field of 30 million volts per metre — strong enough to ionise air. Cells run their lives in fields this intense.
items.prompt: Why is the membrane voltage so high?

options.text: The proton motive force has two components — pH gradient (~1 unit) and electrical potential (~150 mV) — and together they store the energy released by respiration in a form that ATP synthase can harvest
Mitochondria conduct electricity for the cell
Voltage is needed for genetic material to fold

items.reveal:
Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory unified electron transport with ATP synthesis through the proton motive force (PMF). Total PMF (the cell's 'fuel gauge') = chemical potential of proton gradient + electrical potential of charge separation.

Magnitudes in mitochondria: pH gradient is about 0.7 units (intermembrane space more acidic), membrane potential about -150 to -180 mV (matrix is negative). Together: ~200 mV of PMF, or ~20 kJ/mol of proton transferred.

The field strength (~3 x 10^7 V/m) inside the membrane is comparable to lightning. Life happens at electric fields that humans only experience during catastrophes.

Across thylakoid membranes (chloroplasts), the gradient is mostly chemical (pH 5 vs 8) rather than electrical.

Disrupting PMF with uncouplers, ionophores or cyanide kills cells in seconds — the gradient must be continuously rebuilt to maintain ATP synthesis.
items.why: Cells seem soft and slow. The energy machinery within them runs at field strengths that would shatter rigid materials. Life depends on holding lightning-scale electricity inside membranes of fat.

items.title: Bacteria count themselves before acting
items.claim: A single Vibrio fischeri bacterium doesn't glow. A dense colony of them lights up the inside of squid light organs and certain Hawaiian fish. The bacteria sense how many bacteria are around them and only switch on bioluminescence when there are enough to matter.
items.prompt: How does a bacterium know how many others are nearby?

options.text: Quorum sensing — each cell secretes a small molecule (an autoinducer); local concentration of autoinducer rises with population density, and at threshold activates gene expression
They wait a fixed time before turning on

items.reveal:
Quorum sensing was discovered in Vibrio fischeri by Hastings and Nealson in the 1970s. Each bacterium continuously produces and secretes a homoserine lactone. At low cell density it diffuses away; at high density it accumulates, enters cells and binds a transcription factor that activates luciferase genes.

Bonnie Bassler's group showed in the 1990s that many bacteria use multiple quorum signals — one species-specific, one universal (AI-2). The universal one allows cross-species 'eavesdropping' on population density of other bacteria.

Pathogens use quorum sensing to time virulence factor expression: stay quiet until there are enough cells to overwhelm the host. Anti-quorum-sensing drugs are an active research area for antibiotic alternatives.
items.why: Bacteria are imagined as solitary cells acting independently. Many of their key behaviours — virulence, biofilm formation, bioluminescence — are coordinated through chemical signalling networks.
